DEBUGGING
To the uninitiated, debugging can seem like a
mystical art. On the contrary, it's actually one
of the best skills you can have as a developer,
though it's rarely taught to novice coders,
which I think is a tragic missed opportunity.
All coders make mistakes, and knowing about
debugging will enable you to find and correct
those mistakes much faster than just staring at
the code and hoping the bug will reveal itself.
By the end of this chapter, you'll understand
the difference between a compile-time error
and a runtime error, you'll know how to set
breakpoints in your code, and you'll know how
to step through the lines of your program one
at a time to help you root out hard-to-find
bugs.

I've spent so much time helping

common include the following:
■ Misspellings: If you type even one letter wrong, the computer
won't have any idea what you're talking about.
■ Capitalization: To your C# compiler, $ and a are two completely
different letters, so Yariable, 9ariable, and Yari$ble are all

Compile-Time Bugs
A compile-time bug (or error) is a problem that Unity discovers when it is compiling C#
code (i.e., when it is attempting to interpret the C# code and turn it into the Common
Intermediate Language that is later converted by Unity to machine language that can
run on your computer).

automatically increment the name of the scene and call this new scene _Scene_2.

make a couple quick changes. (If you like how Unity numbers things now, you don't
need to do this and can just manually rename _Scene_1 1 to _Scene_2.)

HOW TO FORCE QUIT AN APPLICATION
Before getting too far into debugging, knowing how to force quit an application
(i.e., quit an application that won't respond to any user input) is useful. Some-
times, either Unity or Visual Studio will just stop responding, and you might need
to do this to quit the frozen application.
On a macOS Computer
Implement a force quit by doing the following:
1. Press Command+Option+Esc on the keyboard. The Force Quit window appears.
2. Find the application that is misbehaving. Its name is often followed by "(not
responding)" in the applications list.
3. Click that application, and then click Force Quit.
On a Windows Computer
Implement a force quit by doing the following:
1. Press Shift+Ctrl+Esc on the keyboard. The Windows Task Manager opens.
2. Find the application that is misbehaving.
3. Click that application, and then click the End Task button (in the bottom right).
If you have to force quit Unity while it's running, you will lose any work that
you've done in your scene since your last save. Because you must constantly
save C# scripts, they shouldn't be an issue, but you might have to redo unsaved
changes made to your scene. This is one of the reasons that I encourage you to
save your scenes as often as possible.
Enabling Debugging in Unity 2020
Prior to Unity version 2020, all code within the Unity Editor was always compiled in
Debug mode, allowing you to run the debugger at any time. However, with Unity's
recent moves toward efficiency and stability in the latest versions, all code now com-
piles in Release mode by default. Release mode code is faster and more efficient, but
you cannot attach a debugger to it. In Unity 2020.3, there is a new Debugging button in
the bottom-right of the Unity window that allows you to switch compilation to Debug
mode (shown in Figure 25.8).

One of the great strengths of any debugger is the capability it offers for you to
look at the value of an individual variable at almost any time. Visual Studio's
debugger gives you three different ways to do this. Before trying any of these, be
sure that you've followed the directions in this chapter and started the debugging
process.
Hover the mouse pointer over the variable: The first and simplest method is
to just hover your mouse pointer over any variable in the Visual Studio code pane.
If you position the mouse pointer over a variable name and keep it still for about
one second, a tool tip will appear telling you the value of that variable. However,
it is very important to note that the value shown is the current value of the variable
based on the position of the yellow arrow, not the position of that variable in the
code. For example, the variable sB of the function SpellIt2ut() is repeated
several times throughout the code, and holding the mouse over any of them will
show the same value.
Locals pane: The second method is to find the variable in the Locals pane of the
debugger. To view this pane, from the Visual Studio menu bar, choose View >
Debug Windows > Locals (macOS) or Debug > Windows > Locals (Windows). This
brings the Locals variable watching pane to the front. Here, you can see a list of all
local variables that are available to the debugger at the current time. If you step
into the SpellIt2ut() function as instructed in this chapter and are on line 19,
you will see at least three local variables listed: this, s$, and sB (other variables
may be there as well). The variables s$ and sB are initially set to null, but their
values appear in the Locals pane after they have been defined on lines 19 and 20,
respectively. When you have used Step Over a few times and reached line 22 in
the debugger, you will see that the integer i is both declared and defined on that
line. The variable this refers to the current instance of the CubeSpawner2 script.

Summary
That's it for your introduction to debugging. Although in this case you did not use the
debugger to root out an unknown bug, you can see how it can help you better under-
stand code. Remember this: Whenever something is confusing in your code, you can
always step through it using the debugger.
Though it might have seemed a bit frustrating for me to instruct you to generate so
many bugs, my sincere hope is that helping you to experience and understand these
bugs and how to investigate and fix them will give you a leg up later when you encoun-

text of the bug (or at least the error number) to find clues for fixing it. As I wrote at the
beginning of the chapter, good debugging skills are one of the most important things

The Object-Oriented Metaphor
The easiest way to describe object orientation is through a metaphor. Think about all
the birds in a flock. Flocks can consist of hundreds or even thousands of individual birds,
each of which must avoid obstacles and other birds while still moving along with the
flock. Flocks of birds exhibit brilliantly coordinated behaviors that defied simulation for
many years.
Simulating a Flock of Birds in a Monolithic Way
Before the advent of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), a program was basically
a single large function that did everything.
1
That single function controlled all data,
moved sprites on screen, and handled everything from keyboard input to game logic,
music, and graphics. This attempt to do everything with a single, gigantic function is
now referred to as monolithic programming.
To attempt to simulate a flock of birds in a monolithic way, it would make sense to store
a large array of the birds and create a program that would consider every bird in the
flock and attempt to generate swarming-style behavior for them. This program would
individually move each bird from its position in one frame to its position in the next, and
it would maintain all data about the birds in the array.
A monolithic program like this would be very large, unwieldy, and difficult to debug.
For example, if the EnePy and EnePy=ig classes from the previous chapter were com-
bined into a single monolithic class that controlled all enemies, the code would have
looked like what is shown in Code Listing 27.1.

This preconception was shattered with the publication of the paper "Flocks, Herds,
and Schools: A Distributed Behavioral Model" by Craig W. Reynolds in 1987.

In this
paper, Reynolds described an incredibly simple, object-oriented approach to simulating
swarm-like behavior, which he called Boids. At its most basic level, Boids uses only three
simple rules:
Q Collision avoidance: Avoid collisions with nearby flockmates
Q Velocity matching: Attempt to match velocity with nearby flockmates
Q Flock centering: Attempt to stay near the average location of nearby flockmates
An Object-Oriented Boids
Implementation
In this tutorial, you'll build a simple implementation of Reynolds' Boids that shows the
power of simple object-oriented code to create complex, emergent behavior. First,
create a new project following the instructions in the sidebar.

chunks.heading: COMPONENT-ORIENTED DESIGN
chunks.content:
COMPONENT-ORIENTED DESIGN
The Component Pattern was formalized in the 1994 book Design Patterns: Elements
of Reusable Object-Oriented Software
6
by the "Gang of Four." The core idea of the
Component Pattern is to group closely related functions and data into a single
class while at the same time keeping each class as small and focused as possible.
7
As you might have guessed from the name, you've been working with compo-
nents the whole time you've been using Unity. Each GameObject in Unity is a
very small class that can act as a container for several components that each do a
specific—and isolated—job. For example:
Q Transform handles position, rotation, scale, and hierarchy.
Q Rigidbody handles motion and physics of GameObjects, but not their
collision.
Q Colliders handle actual collision and the shape of the collision volume.
Although each of these is related, they are separate enough to each warrant a sep-
arate component. Making each a component also enables easy expansion in the
future: separating Colliders from the Rigidbody means that we could easily add a
new kind of Collider—a ConeCollider or EllipsoidCollider, for instance—and Rigid-
body would not need to change at all to accommodate the new Collider type.
This is certainly important for game engine developers, but what does it mean to
us as game designers and prototypers? The most important benefit of thinking
in a component-oriented way is smaller, shorter classes. When your scripts are
shorter, they are easier to code, share with other people, reuse, and debug; all of
which are very noble goals.
The only real negative of component-oriented design is that implementing it
well takes a decent amount of forethought, which somewhat flies in the face of
our prototyping philosophy of getting things working as quickly as possible. As
a result of this dilemma, in Part III of this book, you will encounter both a more
traditional prototyping style of just writing what works in the first several chapters
and a much more intentionally component-oriented approach in the chapters for
the Dungeon Delver prototype.
6. Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, and John Vissides, Design Patterns: Elements of
Reusable Object-Oriented Software (Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley, 1994). Design Patterns was
also the book that formalized the Singleton pattern and several others used throughout my
book.
7. The full description of the Component pattern is far more complex, but this will serve our
needs.

HEADERS IN THE INSPECTOR
In Code Listing 27.2, you see an example of the Header compiler attribute. Com-
piler attributes give the compiler in Unity (and Visual Studio) specific commands
and are always contained within brackets (e.g., >Header( Inscribed )@ ).
The Header attribute tells Unity that you want a bold header to appear above the
following public field in the Inspector. Figure 27.8 shows two examples:
Figure 27.8 The Header compiler attribute in C# and how it appears in the Inspector
These are the two most common Headers that I use throughout the rest of this
book:
Q Inscribed: I use the Inscribed header to signify that these fields are
meant to be modified in the Inspector as settings for the component
before clicking Play.
Q Dynamic: In contrast, fields under the Dynamic header are meant to
help you see the current state of the script each frame and are often over-
written by the code every frame. The initial values of these Dynamic fields
(i.e., the values placed in them before clicking Play) almost never matter,
because the code treats these fields as outputs, not inputs.

FIXED UPDATES AND THE PHYSICS ENGINE
Because Unity is trying to run as quickly as possible, it displays a new frame when-
ever possible. This means that the TiPe.deltaTiPe between each 8pdate() can
range anywhere from less than 1/1000 of a second on a fast computer to 1 second
or more on a very slow device. Additionally, the frequency of 8pdate() s changes
drastically from one frame to the next on the same computer based on a number
of factors, so the TiPe.deltaTiPe between each 8pdate() is always different.
Physics engines—like the NVIDIA PhysX engine traditionally used by Unity—rely
on predictability and stability, something that 8pdate() cannot offer. As a result,
Unity has a physics update that always runs at the same rate, regardless of the
